model_claims.text: Constructing a window of size n therefore replays 0 + 1 + ... + (n - 1) cached items before returning.
model_claims.source_quote: Constructing a window of size n therefore replays 0 + 1 + ... + (n - 1) cached items before returning.

model_claims.text: Copy each preceding offset and advance the copy once instead.
model_claims.source_quote: Copy each preceding offset and advance the copy once instead.

model_claims.text: The returned zip still operates directly on tee iterators, retaining the iteration-speed benefit discussed in #321.
model_claims.source_quote: The returned zip still operates directly on tee iterators, retaining the iteration-speed benefit discussed in #321.

model_claims.text: Use the second output of tee: Python 3.9 can reuse the input iterator as its first output.
model_claims.source_quote: Use the second output of tee: Python 3.9 can reuse the input iterator as its first output.

model_claims.text: Tests cover consumption before and after the first yields, infinite inputs, short inputs, a large window, integer-like sizes, zero-size non-consumption, and inputs that are already tee iterators.
model_claims.source_quote: Tests cover consumption before and after the first yields, infinite inputs, short inputs, a large window, integer-like sizes, zero-size non-consumption, and inputs that are already tee iterators.

model_claims.text: A startup benchmark is added alongside the existing sliding-window benchmark.
model_claims.source_quote: A startup benchmark is added alongside the existing sliding-window benchmark.

model_claims.text: For n=500, the median time for next(sliding_window(n, range(n))) dropped from 1.002 ms to 0.142 ms (7.1x speedup).
Consuming 100,000 values with windows of 1, 3 and 16 stayed within about 4% of the original timings.

model_claims.text: At n=8000, tracemalloc peak increased from 1,024,232 to 1,088,384 bytes (about 6%), including construction and the first result.
model_claims.source_quote: At n=8000, tracemalloc peak increased from 1,024,232 to 1,088,384 bytes (about 6%), including construction and the first result.

model_claims.text: Both implementations retain O(n) iterator/cache space.

claims.text: Constructing a window of size n therefore replays 0 + 1 + ... + (n - 1) cached items before returning.
Copy each preceding offset and advance the copy once instead.
The returned zip still operates directly on tee iterators, retaining the iteration-speed benefit discussed in #321.
Use the second output of tee: Python 3.9 can reuse the input iterator as its first output.
Tests cover consumption before and after the first yields, infinite inputs, short inputs, a large window, integer-like sizes, zero-size non-consumption, and inputs that are already tee iterators.
A startup benchmark is added alongside the existing sliding-window benchmark.
For n=500, the median time for next(sliding_window(n, range(n))) dropped from 1.002 ms to 0.142 ms (7.1x speedup).
Consuming 100,000 values with windows of 1, 3 and 16 stayed within about 4% of the original timings.
At n=8000, tracemalloc peak increased from 1,024,232 to 1,088,384 bytes (about 6%), including construction and the first result.
Both implementations retain O(n) iterator/cache space.
